concepts.title: Apparent Motion

position.section_title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

concepts.one_liner: Apparent motion is the illusion of continuous movement created by displaying a sequence of static images.
concepts.content: Apparent motion refers to the phenomenon where the human visual system perceives continuous motion from a sequence of static images. This discovery from cognitive psychology has significantly impacted imaging technology, most notably in the creation of movies.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how the brain perceives motion allows engineers to create fluid visual experiences, like film and video, using only a series of still frames.
concepts.recap_md: - Apparent motion is the psychological phenomenon of perceiving movement in a sequence of static frames.

key_passage.text: The fact that we learned to create the illusion of continuous motion by displaying a sequence of static images (a phenomenon called apparent motion) was a remarkable discovery.

concepts.title: Waterfall Illusion

position.section_title: Motion Perception in the Human Visual System

concepts.one_liner: The waterfall illusion is a motion aftereffect where staring at constant motion causes a subsequent static texture to appear to drift in the opposite direction.
concepts.content: The waterfall illusion is a famous visual illusion associated with motion perception. When an observer looks at constant motion, such as a waterfall, the brain adapts to that motion. If the observer immediately looks at a static texture after this adaptation, the texture appears to drift in the opposite direction. This phenomenon was known to the ancient Greeks and was reported by Aristotle.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion provides insight into how the brain's motion detectors adapt to stimuli, helping researchers understand the underlying neural mechanisms of vision.
concepts.recap_md: - The illusion occurs when the brain adapts to constant motion, causing static objects to appear to move in the opposite direction.

key_passage.text: When looking at a constant motion (such as a waterfall) our brain adapts to the motion in such a way that if, immediately after adaptation, we look at a static texture we will see it drifting in the opposite direction.

motivation.text: There are a number of visual illusions associated with motion perception that are intriguing and offer a window into how motion perception is implemented in the brain.

concepts.one_liner: The Rotating Snakes illusion uses static images with specific patterns to produce a sensation of motion.
concepts.content: The Rotating Snakes visual illusion, created by cognitive psychologist Akiyoshi Kitaoka, demonstrates that static images can produce a sensation of motion. (see figure: Motion-induced visual illusion, after @Murakami2010. The illusion becomes stronger when viewed peripherally rather than looking directly at the image. The effect uses simple elements to induce the illusion and typically becomes more intense as the viewer moves their eyes to explore different parts of the image or views it peripherally.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion demonstrates that motion perception is not just about tracking moving objects, but can be triggered by specific spatial patterns and eye movements.
concepts.recap_md: - This illusion creates a perceived sense of rotation from a completely static image.

concepts.title: Hassenstein-Reichardt Model
concepts.one_liner: The Hassenstein-Reichardt model is an early computational model of motion perception based on the fly's visual system.
concepts.content: The Hassenstein-Reichardt model is one of the earliest computational models of motion perception. It was proposed by Hassenstein and Reichardt in 1956 following their studies of motion detectors within the visual system of flies.
concepts.motivation_md: By studying simpler biological systems like the fly, researchers could develop the first mathematical frameworks for how neurons might detect the direction and speed of motion.
concepts.recap_md: - It is a foundational computational model for biological motion detection.

concepts.title: Adelson-Bergen Energy Model
concepts.one_liner: The Adelson-Bergen energy model is a computational framework for human motion perception.
concepts.content: The energy model proposed by Adelson and Bergen in 1985 is a computational model designed to explain human motion perception. It is often discussed in the context of filter banks and how the visual system extracts motion energy from stimuli.
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a way to understand how the human brain processes motion as a spatiotemporal energy signal, rather than just tracking discrete features.
concepts.recap_md: - The model characterizes motion perception through the lens of spatiotemporal energy filters.

concepts.title: Matching-Based Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Matching-based motion estimation computes pixel displacement between video frames by finding corresponding color patches.
concepts.content: Matching-based motion estimation computes the displacement of pixels between two video frames by finding correspondences. (see figure: Frame 1) (see figure: Frame 2) Because individual pixel colors are often not distinctive enough, each pixel is represented by a color patch of size $C=3\times(2s+1)\times(2s+1)$ centered on the pixel. For a pixel at $(n,m)$ in image $\boldsymbol\ell$, the patch is $\boldsymbol\ell[n-s:n+s, m-s:m+s]$. Small values of $s$ may be less distinctive, while large values may fail if there is significant geometric distortion. To simplify matching, we often assume small motion and search only within a neighborhood of size $L \times L$ in the second frame. The algorithm computes the Euclidean distance between patches and selects the one with the smallest distance. (see figure: Patch matching motion estimation. The algorithm starts by chopping the two frames into overlapping patches. Then, for every patch from the first frame, we compute the distance to all the nearby...) (see figure: Two frames and best match for an input patch from frame 1 within frame 2. Search is done only within a small neighborhood.) The choice of patch size $s$ is critical: very small patches result in noisy motion fields, while very large patches can cause motion to 'bleed' across object boundaries. (see figure: Effect of the choice of the patch size parameter, $s$, on the estimated optical flow. When the patch size is just one pixel ($s=0$), the approach fails as there are many similar pixels that...) This approach is independent of object types and can serve as a cue for grouping, though it typically lacks subpixel accuracy and struggles at motion discontinuities.
concepts.motivation_md: Estimating how objects move between frames is fundamental for video compression, tracking, and autonomous navigation. Patch matching provides a straightforward way to estimate this motion without needing to pre-segment objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Motion is estimated by finding the best-matching patch in a subsequent frame using Euclidean distance.

key_passage.text: Under this formulation, the task of motion estimation consists of finding, for each pixel in frame 1, the location of the corresponding pixel in frame 2. Just as in the chapter on stereo matching, we need first to define how we will compare pixels to find correspondences.

concepts.title: Human Motion Perception and the Fluted Square-Wave Illusion

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: The fluted square-wave illusion distinguishes between pattern matching and spatiotemporal filtering, supporting the theory that the human visual system uses spatiotemporal energy models.
concepts.content: While researchers aren't sure of the precise computations involved in human motion processing, experiments can distinguish between classes of algorithms the visual system may use. Pattern matching methods are often based on image correlations, while spatiotemporal filtering uses the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion. Adelson and Bergen proposed the fluted square-wave illusion to distinguish between these classes. The illusion involves temporal filtering, motion processing, and aliasing. A stationary sinusoid $f(x,y,t) = \cos(\pi \omega x)$ has a spatiotemporal Fourier transform $(\delta(w_x + \omega) + \delta(w_x - \omega)) \delta(w_y) \delta(w_t)$, with energy along the $w_t = 0$ line. A moving sinusoid shears this energy according to speed. A square wave moving in 1/4 period jumps creates a spectrum replicated over temporal frequencies. (see figure: Derivation of the fluted square-wave motion illusion, continued from @fig-motionIllusion1 . Top row shows that the square wave moves in 1/4 wavelength jumps, instead of continuously. This staggered...) Because orientation in space-time tells motion direction, the space-time plot of @fig-motionIllusion2 [b] shows motion to the left. However, if the lowest spatial frequency sinusoid is removed, the lowest spatiotemporal frequency component is oriented in the other direction. While pattern matching would still suggest leftward motion, the human visual system perceives rightward motion, supporting spatiotemporal energy models.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between matching and filtering models helps researchers understand the underlying computations of human motion perception and design more effective computer vision systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Pattern matching and spatiotemporal filtering are two primary theories for human motion perception.

key_passage.text: Adelson and Bergen proposed a beautiful motion illusion that distinguishes between two classes of motion algorithms that might be used by the visual system. The illusion involves temporal filtering, motion processing, and aliasing and thus provides a good review of the material in this chapter and also chapters on sampling and temporal filters.

concepts.title: Pattern Matching Methods

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: Pattern matching methods are a class of motion estimation algorithms that are typically based on image correlations.
concepts.content: Pattern matching methods are a class of algorithms that the visual system may use for motion estimation. These methods are often based on calculating image correlations to find correspondences between frames.
concepts.motivation_md: These methods provide a direct way to estimate motion by finding the most similar local image patches across different time steps.
concepts.recap_md: - Pattern matching is a fundamental approach to motion estimation.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Filtering

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal filtering is a motion estimation approach that utilizes the responses of velocity-tuned filters.
concepts.content: Spatiotemporal filtering is a class of motion algorithms that uses the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion. These principles involve analyzing signals across both spatial and temporal dimensions simultaneously.
concepts.motivation_md: Spatiotemporal filtering allows for motion estimation by treating a video sequence as a single 3D volume, capturing dynamic patterns that simple matching might miss.
concepts.recap_md: - This method estimates motion using filters tuned to specific velocities.

key_passage.text: Spatiotemporal filtering uses the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate the motion.

prereq.rationale: The Hassenstein-Reichardt model is a computational explanation for how biological systems perceive apparent motion.
Matching-based estimation is a specific implementation of the general correspondence problem in motion.
The fluted square-wave illusion was specifically proposed by Adelson and Bergen to support their energy model of motion processing.

overlay.rationale: Both are foundational computational models of biological motion perception, often compared in vision science.
This definition provides a formal computational framework for the phenomenon of apparent motion.
While apparent motion involves perceiving movement from a sequence of images, the waterfall illusion involves perceiving movement in a static image due to prior adaptation.
Both are visual illusions where motion is perceived in the absence of actual physical movement in the stimulus.
Spatiotemporal filtering is the broader class of motion algorithms that includes specific implementations like the Adelson-Bergen energy model.
